body.objective: Students will be able to lead a sectional rehearsal.
body.iCan: I can lead a sectional rehearsal.
successCriteria: I can plan and lead a short sectional rehearsal
I can identify and fix problems with clear, kind feedback
I can play independently in a small ensemble without a conductor
body.hook: In a professional orchestra, the principal of each section leads without saying much: a nod, a breath, a lifted bell. In a high school band, section leaders run sectionals, fix problems and help the whole group get better faster.

vocabulary.definition: The player who leads and guides their section.
A rehearsal of one section without the full band.
A list of goals and steps for a rehearsal.
A small group with one player per part, often without a conductor.
A visual signal (breath, nod, instrument movement) to start or change together.
Playing your part confidently without relying on others.

study.title: Leading from the Chair
study.question: How do section leaders and chamber players rehearse without a conductor?
study.passage:
Part 1, Plan (10 minutes): Section leaders choose 16 bars from a band piece. Plan a 20-minute sectional: tune (2 minutes), identify the two hardest spots, fix them (slow, chunk, then in context), run the 16 bars, set one goal for home practice.
Part 2, Lead (20 minutes): Leaders run the sectional. Feedback rules: name the bar, name the problem, give a fix ("Bar 23, the eighths are rushing; let's play it at 60 with the metronome"). Praise something specific.
Part 3, Chamber skills (15 minutes): Form trios or quartets (one per part). Choose a leader who gives the cue: a big breath and a nod on the upbeat before the first note. Practise starting together, ending together (watch the leader's instrument lift and drop), and changing tempo.
Part 4, Reflect (5 minutes): What did the leader do that helped? What will you do differently next time?
study.source: Original leadership workshop written for this lesson.

examples.title: Feedback
examples.problem: Rewrite "That was bad" as useful feedback.
examples.answer: "Bar 12, the entrance was late; let's count the rest aloud and try again"

examples.title: Rehearsal order
examples.problem: Why tune before working on passages?
examples.answer: Tuning first means you fix notes and rhythms on a good sound

examples.title: Cue
examples.problem: How does a chamber group start together?
examples.answer: The leader breathes and nods on the upbeat
examples.explore: What if someone misses the cue?

examples.title: Independence
examples.problem: Your part is different from everyone else in a quartet. How do you prepare?
examples.answer: Learn your part securely and listen to recordings to know how it fits

practice.a: A rehearsal of one section only.
The player who leads their section.
A small group with one player per part.
A visual signal to start or change together.
A list of goals and steps for a rehearsal.

practice.q: Name the three parts of useful feedback.
How should you fix a hard passage?
practice.a: Slow it down, chunk it, then put it back in context.

practice.q: How does a chamber leader cue the start?
practice.a: A breath and nod on the upbeat.

practice.q: Why set a home-practice goal at the end of a sectional?
practice.a: So progress continues before the next rehearsal.
It shows what to keep doing and builds confidence.

practice.q: Why does each player need independence in chamber music?
practice.a: There is only one person per part.

practice.q: How can a section leader handle a player who keeps making the same mistake?
practice.a: Give a clear fix privately, practise slowly together, encourage.

practice.q: Why do chamber musicians make eye contact?
practice.a: To communicate cues, tempo and expression without a conductor.
A clear plan focused on the hardest spots.

practice.q: How does leadership in music build skills for other areas?
practice.a: Planning, communication, feedback and teamwork transfer to school and work.

misconceptions: Thinking leading means telling people they are wrong
Running a piece over and over instead of fixing problem spots
Thinking chamber players don't need a leader
exitTicket: Write one piece of feedback with bar, problem and fix.
Describe how to cue a chamber group.

items.q: Define sectional.
items.answer: A rehearsal of one section without the full band.

items.q: What is a cue?
items.answer: A visual signal to start or change together.

items.q: Write a 20-minute sectional plan.
items.answer: Answers vary; tune, fix hard spots, run, set goal.

items.q: Give an example of useful feedback.
items.answer: Answers vary; bar, problem, fix.

items.q: How do chamber groups stay together without a conductor?
items.answer: Visual cues, eye contact, breathing and listening.
